extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy; readers interested in theories of constitution and government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's criteria for constitutions, offices, and the allocation of political power — i.e., standards for judging what makes laws, magistrates, and regimes just or effective. Useful for comparative assessment of governmental forms and institutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme power lodged in laws duly made
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme power should be lodged in laws duly made and the magistrate(s) should be authorised to determine those cases which the laws cannot particularly speak to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws must be the primary repository of supreme power; magistrates have delegated discretion only to decide particulars that fall outside the general language of laws. The existence of written law is essential for consistent governance, though some particulars require magistratial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must correspond to the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of every state will necessarily be like every state, either trifling or excellent, just or unjust; the laws must be framed correspondent to the constitution of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good laws are those fitted to the state's constitution. A well-formed government will tend to produce good laws; a bad constitution, bad laws. Legislative design should account for the character and structure of the polity it serves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as equality — determine equals and unequals
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is a certain equality; equals ought to receive equal. We must know how to determine what things are equal and what unequal — this requires the politician's philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of justice require a principled method for deciding relevant similarity (who counts as 'equal') so that distributive and corrective measures allocate benefits and burdens appropriately. Superficial or irrelevant traits should not be treated as bases of equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of offices by relevant excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Employments of the state ought to be given according to every particular excellence of each citizen insofar as that excellence relates to the office; superiority in unrelated qualities (e.g., beauty, family) is no claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices should be filled by those who possess the specific capacities useful to that office (e.g., best flute to best flautist). Avoid awarding political office on irrelevant merits such as birth, complexion, or wealth unless those qualities bear on the public function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular share in government for certain powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Freemen who compose the bulk of the people should have absolute power in some things; they should be permitted to vote in public assemblies, determine causes, elect officers, and inquire into conduct, though not necessarily be magistrates themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of the many in assemblies and judicial determinations secures social stability (prevents many enemies within the state) and harnesses collective understanding; nevertheless, entrusting the highest offices to the unqualified is unsafe because of ignorance and iniquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence-based election by those skilled
rubrics_metrics.description: To elect a proper person in any science is the business of those who are skilful therein; as in geometry, geometricians should judge; in steering, steersmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where specialized knowledge matters, selection/assessment should rest with practitioners or those competent to judge the art. Anti-pattern: letting lay majorities choose technical officers when they lack the requisite understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective judgement preferred to individual judgement for many matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When the people come together they will know matters better, or at least not worse, than any one individual; the multitude judge many things better than any single person, and are less liable to corruption from their numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For cases where mass deliberation can aggregate information and blunt individual passion, prefer decisions by many (assemblies, councils) over rule by a single ruler. But beware division among the many where unanimity of virtue is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law over ruler — law as reason without desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Law is reason without desire; it is more proper that law should govern than any one of the citizens. The best magistrates should be guardians and servants of the laws, not arbitrary masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design should prioritize rule of law rather than rule by individuals, because laws provide an impartial mean and constrain passions. Even a good ruler must be subordinate to law; the legislator's aim is to make laws govern general life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrates to decide particulars not covered by law
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates should be authorised to determine those cases which the laws cannot particularly speak to, because general language cannot explain everything that may arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide institutional roles for discretionary adjudication where written law is silent or vague; but such discretion should be limited and guided by legal principles to prevent arbitrary rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ostracism and constitutional remedies for excessive pre-eminence
rubrics_metrics.description: When any persons are too eminent in power, fortune, friendships, or other causes that give them too great weight in the government, it is politically just to restrain and banish them (ostracism) to preserve equality and prevent tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions may legitimately include mechanisms to check individuals who become disproportionately powerful. However, such devices can be abused for factional gain and should ideally be unnecessary if the state is well structured from the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws are aimed at ordinary citizens, not exceptional individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of laws must be calculated for those who are equal to each other in nature and power; very eminent individuals whose virtue makes them 'a law' unto themselves are not the object of ordinary law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design legal codes for the general populace; exceptional persons of overwhelming virtue or authority fall outside normal regulation — either they will rule by consent or must be handled by different political arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute monarchy unjust among equals
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems unnatural and unjust that, where people are equal, one person should have entire rule over his fellow-citizens when his will is the law (absolute monarchy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political equality among citizens implies that absolute, unchecked rule by a single person is inappropriate. Institutional constraints (laws, shared offices) are preferred where natural equality exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: King's coercive power must be balanced
rubrics_metrics.description: The king ought to have proper power sufficient to make him superior to any one person or large part of the community, but inferior to the whole; he must have power to compel obedience to laws while being constrained by the community and law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design executive force strong enough to enforce order and protect the constitution, yet limited so the ruler cannot dominate the whole body politic. Guards or subordinate officials may be necessary, but ultimate accountability must be preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue and education as bases for political office
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue and education most justly claim the right of being considered as the necessary means of making the citizens happy; those qualities have a rightful claim to be considered in selecting rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise moral character and proper education in choosing political leaders because they contribute to the common good and stability. But also consider the number of suitably virtuous persons available — many or few affects regime form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awarding political office on incommensurable excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absurd to claim offices on grounds such as complexion, height, or family, since these excellences have no reference to the business in hand; only superiority in qualifications useful to the office should count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent conflating unrelated personal attributes with political merit. Establish selection criteria tied specifically to the tasks and skills required by the public office to avoid arbitrary or hereditary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual suitability of regime type
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms of government (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy, oligarchy, tyranny) suit different peoples and circumstances; the legislator must consider what people are best qualified for a kingly, aristocratic, or democratic government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose institutional forms responsive to the character, size, and moral condition of the citizenry. One-size-fits-all solutions are inappropriate; regime design should match the nature and capacities of the governed.
